Green water after a storm, a pump that went quiet, a crust of white scale on the tile. Dial one free number at any hour and the call goes to a locally owned, independent pool company serving your part of the Tucson area.

Call (520) 372-1083 How the free line works

One number for pool service in Tucson

When you need swimming pool service in Tucson, the hard part is often just reaching someone. Messages go unanswered, and the water keeps getting worse while you wait.

Tucson Pool Cleaning Pro exists to shorten that wait. It is a free phone line and this website, and nothing more. It is not a pool company. Nobody from the line will ever stand at your pool, carry a test kit, haul chemicals or turn a wrench. It answers your call, asks you briefly what the trouble is, and passes you to a pool company near you that is independent and owned by local people.

From that point on, your business is with that company. It comes out, explains what it finds, sets its own price, does the job and sends you the bill. You owe the line nothing. Pool companies can pay the line for referrals, a fact disclosed on every page of this site.

Why Tucson pools need steady attention

A pool in the Sonoran Desert works harder than a pool almost anywhere else in the country. Four local conditions explain why weekly care is the habit for so many Tucson owners.

Heat and sun

National Weather Service normals for Tucson put the average July high at about 100 degrees, with 68 days a year reaching 100 or more. Warm water grows algae faster, and strong sunlight breaks chlorine down. That is why most outdoor pools here carry cyanuric acid, a stabilizer that shields chlorine from the sun. The CDC advises keeping free chlorine at 2 parts per million or more when stabilizer is in the water.

Monsoon storms and dust

Officially, the Tucson monsoon season runs from June 15 to the end of September, according to the weather service. Thunderstorm outflow can push walls of dust across the desert, and the storms that follow drop leaves, twigs and rain into the water. Filters load up, chlorine gets used up, and a pool that looked fine on Friday can be cloudy by Monday. If yours has already gone green, start with what to do when the pool is green.

Hard fill water

Tucson Water takes its share of Colorado River water, which arrives by canal through the Central Arizona Project (CAP), and sinks it into the aquifer in Avra Valley, where it blends with groundwater before it is pumped to homes. The utility says the water gets harder as the share of CAP water rises, and that hard water is safe to drink. In a pool, those minerals are what form the white crust along the tile and the scale inside heaters and salt cells. Tucson Water suggests testing pool water hardness with a test kit. Pool tile cleaning covers the crust once it builds up.

Evaporation

The Arizona Department of Water Resources puts open-water evaporation in Tucson at about six feet a year, most of it in summer. Every inch that leaves as vapor leaves its minerals behind, and the top-up water brings in more. Over the years that is why many pools eventually need part of their water replaced. According to ADWR, covering the pool keeps 90 to 95 percent of that water from escaping. The guide to draining or recycling pool water in Tucson explains the local rules on where that water may go.

Where the line takes calls

The line covers the City of Tucson and the communities around it in Pima County. Five of them have their own page about the local water, power and pool rules.

Tucson

Midtown, the east and west sides, the northwest and the southeast neighborhoods all call the same number. Inside city limits, Tucson Water and City of Tucson rules on draining and backwash apply.

North of the city

Oro Valley runs its own water utility, and the Catalina Foothills sit below the Santa Catalina Mountains. Marana has no page of its own, but its calls are welcome.

South and southeast

Vail, Sahuarita and Green Valley each have several water providers, and power comes from TEP or Trico depending on the address.

Check a company before work starts

The company you are connected with is independent, so vetting it is up to you, and it only takes a few minutes. For weekly care, ask what each visit includes and who buys the chemicals. For any repair, get the quote on paper, plus the company's Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC) license number to search online. The ROC does not require pool contractors to carry liability insurance, so ask to see proof of it. The how it works page has a short checklist.

Look up the contractor license. Contractor licensing in Arizona is handled by the state Registrar of Contractors, known as the ROC. A residential R-6 license, Swimming Pool Service and Repair, is the one meant for servicing home pools and making minor repairs; building a pool or replacing a whole plaster or pebble interior falls under construction licenses such as B-5. Whether a cleaning-only route needs any license is not spelled out by the ROC, so it is fair to ask a company what it holds. Write down its ROC number and enter it in the state's license lookup (new tab), which lists the license status, classification and recent complaints. Tucson Pool Cleaning Pro does not run this check on anyone.

Common questions

Who shows up when I call for pool service in Tucson?

A locally owned pool company, independent of this site, that takes calls for your side of town. Tucson Pool Cleaning Pro only answers the phone and hands the call over. It sends nobody, owns no equipment and sets no prices. Inspection, the quote, the work and the invoice all come from the company. The how it works page walks through every step.

What is the best pool service in Tucson?

This site does not rank, rate or review pool companies, and it will not tell you one is the best. What it can do is show you how to judge one yourself: get the company's Arizona ROC license number and search it on the ROC website, ask for proof of liability insurance, and get the price and the scope of a weekly plan in writing. The services page explains what each kind of job should include.

Does it cost anything to call the line?

No. The call and the transfer are free, and the line never sends you a bill. Weekly care, a cleanup or a repair is priced by the pool company itself, so ask what the first visit costs before anyone comes. The line may be paid a referral fee by the companies. For published price ranges, read the Tucson pool service cost guide.

Can I call late at night or on a holiday?

Yes. The automated assistant picks up 24 hours a day, every day of the year. If the company cannot come to the phone right then, the assistant passes along who you are, the number to reach you, your area and what the pool is doing, so the company can return the call. When it can actually come out, and what an after-hours visit costs, is the company's call.

How often should a Tucson pool be serviced?

Many owners here choose a weekly visit, because summer heat, strong sun and monsoon dust use up chlorine and clog filters quickly. Some go every other week in the cooler months. The right schedule depends on your pool, your trees and how much you swim. The Tucson pool maintenance schedule breaks it down by season.
